title: Does anyone actually want to win the medium-lift race in the United States?
gist: Eric Berger ranks four US medium-lift rockets in development (Stoke Nova, Relativity Terran R, Rocket Lab Neutron, Firefly/Northrop Eclipse) and gives predicted debut dates between July 2027 and 2029. The race matters because SpaceX plans to pull Falcon 9 from the commercial market as soon as 2028.

themes.theme: Why the medium-lift race matters now

insights.claim: SpaceX withdrawing Falcon 9 from the commercial market as soon as 2028 turns the new medium-lift race from a prestige contest into one where fortunes are made and startups saved.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: A demand vacuum for mid-size launch benefits whichever vehicle first reaches reliable cadence.
insights.quote: the “race” to bring new medium-lift capacity into service is for more than bragging rights.

insights.claim: Satellite operators do not know whom to book with for 2027 to 2030 because Vulcan and New Glenn manifests are stacked and expensive for small and mid-size payloads, while the new rockets are unproven.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Launch scarcity could raise prices and favor operators with secured capacity.
insights.quote: Satellite operators legitimately don’t know who to book launches with in the 2027 to 2030 timeframe

insights.claim: The new US medium-lift generation all build engines in-house, a lesson taken from Falcon 9, in contrast to Antares with Soviet-era engines and a Ukrainian-built core.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Vertical integration of engines is now the baseline for credible launch startups.

insights.claim: Stoke Space's Nova is the most ambitious (fully reusable, novel upper stage, full-flow staged combustion first stage) but is making credible progress, with a predicted debut of July 2027 against a company target of early 2027.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Stoke is a leading candidate to be first to market, though full reusability adds technical risk.

insights.claim: Relativity's Terran R is nominally larger than medium-lift (33.5 t expendable, about 20 t reusable) and was revived by Eric Schmidt's acquisition; with all 13 Aeon R engines acceptance-tested, Berger predicts September 2027.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Billionaire funding rescued the program; execution on reuse economics is the open question.

insights.claim: Rocket Lab's Neutron has slipped due to Archimedes engine problems and difficulties building very large carbon-composite domes out of autoclave, leading Berger to predict January 2028 versus a company target of 2027.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Neutron timing risk matters for Rocket Lab's growth narrative.

insights.claim: Firefly/Northrop's Eclipse is the least certain, with little public discussion of stage hardware and likely partnership friction between a new-space and a traditional company, so Berger leans pessimistic with a no-earlier-than 2029 debut.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Eclipse is the likeliest of the four to miss the post-Falcon 9 window.
insights.quote: Typically, that means things aren’t going well or quickly.
